summary.text: 净 means “clean,” “pure,” or “cleanse.” It is the standardized simplified form of 凈. Historical dictionary accounts distinguish a graph for cleanliness from a separate graph for a moat, but do not explain how this simplified spelling came to represent the cleanliness word.

formation.text: Historical accounts give two distinct constructions for 淨: the graph for a moat by Lu’s north gate combines 水, meaning water, with 爭 as a sound element; the graph for “without dirt” combines 水 with 靜 as a sound element. These accounts do not establish the original construction of 净 from its visible parts 冫 and 争.

history.text: The historical accounts distinguish the moat graph from the cleanliness graph and assign them different sound elements. They do not document a continuous early graphic sequence for 净.
净 is the standardized simplified counterpart of 凈. That graphic relationship does not explain how 净 came to represent the cleanliness word.

uncertainties.text: The connection between 净’s visible parts and the historical cleanliness graph 淨, and the path by which 净 acquired the cleanliness meanings, are unresolved. A commentary derives the moat name from 爭門, but that explanation is not independently corroborated.

senses.text: A cleanliness sense is cited in Mozi. This attestation does not show that cleanliness was the graph’s original meaning.
Historical examples use the word for making something clean and washing it clean. Their chronology and relation to the other recorded senses are unresolved.

senses.gloss: pure or undiluted; entirely gone; other recorded senses
senses.text: Dictionary examples include “pure” or “undiluted” and “exhausted” or “entirely gone.” The evidence does not establish a continuous development among these senses.
Modern character records give these meanings for 净.

developments.text: Both senses are attested, but their relationship is unresolved.

limitations.text: The cited examples do not provide a complete chronology or explain how the spelling 净 acquired these meanings.

evidence.field: 說文釋形、釋義、歷代字書條目
evidence.text: For 淨 (U+6DE8), the dictionary gives two distinct Shuowen entries: ‘魯北城門池也。从水，爭聲’ (the moat by Lu’s north city gate; water semantic element, 爭 phonetic) and ‘無垢薉也。从水，靜聲’ (without dirt; water semantic element, 靜 phonetic). It dates the cleanliness sense to Mozi, 節葬下, and cites Guangyun’s ‘無垢也’. This does not establish that 净’s visible 争 was part of the ancient graphic form, nor that the character originated with the cleanliness sense.
evidence.title: [A02245] 淨 - 教育部《異體字字典》

evidence.text: The entry records 淨 as ‘魯北城門池也。从水，爭聲’, with Shuowen fanqie 士耕切 and a Guangyun entry 疾政切. Its editors say the cleanliness character was originally 瀞, citing Shuowen ‘無垢薉也’, Duan Yucai’s identification of that as the present 淨, and examples: Mozi, 明鬼下 (‘不淨潔’), Guoyu, 周語中 (‘淨其巾冪’, annotated ‘潔也’), and Qi Min Yao Shu (‘治地令淨’; ‘汲水淨洗’). Later examples include pure/undiluted or net senses, and exhausted/entirely gone; these are dictionary-selected examples, not a complete dated chronology.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫

evidence.field: 康熙字典、說文解字注、字義
evidence.text: Separates 凈’s Kangxi gloss ‘冷貌’ (cold in appearance; fanqie 楚耕切) from the cleanliness sense. Its Shuowen commentary treats 淨 as the moat by Lu’s north gate, with 爭 as phonetic and 水 as semantic, and says contemporary usage applies it to 瀞 (‘無垢薉也’). This supports a historical distinction between 凈 and 淨/瀞 senses; modern 净 combines uses associated with 淨, while 凈 has an independently recorded cold sense. The source’s additional claim that the moat’s name 凈 derives from 爭門 is its commentary, not independently established here.

context.provenance: Base evidence consists of imported local JSONL excerpts. Source names identify upstream datasets; extraction may lose sense and language boundaries. Further external evidence and research activity are documented separately in the dossier.
editorial_rules: Write about the character's graphic history; distinguish it from the history of a spoken word.
Separate historical explanation from mnemonics. Do not infer history from modern shapes or readings.
Sources may repeat one another. A source count is not independent corroboration.
Treat Shuowen as a historical account, not automatic confirmation. Its generated English glosses are excluded.
Unrelated word senses may appear in Wiktionary excerpts. Do not merge them into a character origin.
Related-character evidence retains its record_character. Do not silently transfer a traditional form's components to a simplified form.
No glyph image has been visually inspected in this packet. Do not claim to have inspected one.
Explain missing evidence explicitly, especially for Japanese-created characters. A Chinese spelling pronunciation is not evidence for a Japanese origin.

gaps: No primary or character-specific evidence inspected here establishes an oracle-bone or bronze form for 淨/凈; the accessible sources identify Shuowen entries and small-seal material but do not expose the underlying glyph images for this inquiry. Do not assert a continuous graphic evolution or call the form corrupt on this evidence.

The two Shuowen entries are distinct: the moat-name graph is analyzed 从水、爭聲; the cleanliness graph is analyzed 从水、靜聲 and is identified by later commentary with modern 淨. How the modern simplified spelling 净—with visible 冫 and 争—came to be used for cleanliness should not be projected backward as its original semantic/phonetic construction. The official simplification page was inaccessible at the needed character entry.

Modern 凈 has Mandarin readings jìng and zhēng in CNS11643, while the local HSK extract has neither character and official Unihan pages failed to open. No ancient pronunciation comparison within a single reconstruction system was verified, so no historical phonetic matching between 争 and 净 is asserted.

The exact chronology and semantic bridge from a named Lu moat to senses such as clean, pure, cleanse, all/only, and theatrical role are not fully established by this bounded source inspection. The sources attest examples in Mozi, Guoyu, Qi Min Yao Shu, Song sources, Tang poetry, and later works, but do not resolve whether all developments are continuous semantic extensions, graphic substitution, or borrowing.

A dictionary commentary derives the moat name from the gate name 爭門 and notes a competing/related form 埩, but this etymology was not independently corroborated. No separate graph-loan claim is needed or demonstrated for the modern clean sense.
The local repository files baxtersagart.tsv and full Unihan_Readings.txt were absent. Exact local readings could not be cross-checked; no Baxter–Sagart forms are repeated here.

No recommendation to store a local source extract: the research used character-specific dictionary pages and upstream variant lines; a bulk extract license and a clear repeatability benefit for this narrow record were not verified.

No usable, character-specific historical glyph image with verifiable direct image URL and reuse provenance was established after searching Xiaoxuetang and Wikimedia Commons. The Xiaoxuetang rights notice is CC0 for query-interface glyph images, but the queried 淨 evolution record was inaccessible in this run; the chardb.iis.sinica.edu.tw character page is all rights reserved.

Accessible primary dictionary evidence supports two distinct Shuowen analyses: moat graph with 爭 phonetic and cleanliness graph with 靜 phonetic. It does not show how the modern simplified spelling 净 became associated with the cleanliness senses; do not project its visible 冫 and 争 backward as the original graphic analysis.
No oracle-bone or bronze attestation was personally inspected. The Ministry of Education entry marks some paleographic resources unavailable, and the attempted Academia Sinica evolution page failed.

The official Unicode character endpoints for both 净 and 凈 failed in the web tool; local HSK1 data has no rows, and full Unihan_Readings.txt and baxtersagart.tsv are absent per dossier. A secondary mirror lists 凈 as jìng, but this is not official click-through evidence. No historic phonetic comparison is asserted.
The bounded searches did not establish exact dates for the earliest cited Mozi cleanliness usage or a continuous semantic path from moat name to clean, all/entirely, or theatrical-role senses.
No tracked local extract recommended: the character-specific evidence does not establish bulk-reuse terms or clear repeatability value.

limitations.text: No historical glyph image is included because the available candidates do not establish an inspectable, character-specific glyph with a verifiable source and reuse provenance. The historical dictionary evidence distinguishes a moat graph analyzed with 爭 as phonetic from a cleanliness graph analyzed with 靜 as phonetic, but does not document an early glyph sequence for modern 净.

The Xiaoxuetang rights notice is CC0 for query-interface glyph images, but the queried 淨 evolution record was inaccessible in this run; the chardb.iis.sinica.edu.tw character page is all rights reserved.

Accessible primary dictionary evidence supports two distinct Shuowen analyses: moat graph with 爭 phonetic and cleanliness graph with 靜 phonetic. It does not show how the modern simplified spelling 净 became associated with the cleanliness senses; do not project its visible 冫 and 争 backward as the original graphic analysis.
No oracle-bone or bronze attestation was personally inspected. The Ministry of Education entry marks some paleographic resources unavailable, and the attempted Academia Sinica evolution page failed.

The official Unicode character endpoints for both 净 and 凈 failed in the web tool; local HSK1 data has no rows, and full Unihan_Readings.txt and baxtersagart.tsv are absent per dossier. A secondary mirror lists 凈 as jìng, but this is not official click-through evidence. No historic phonetic comparison is asserted.
The bounded searches did not establish exact dates for the earliest cited Mozi cleanliness usage or a continuous semantic path from moat name to clean, all/entirely, or theatrical-role senses.
No tracked local extract recommended: the character-specific evidence does not establish bulk-reuse terms or clear repeatability value.
